Chapter 10: Looking Back—Reflections on Hope, Change, and the Human Spirit
You know, time has this gentle way of smoothing out our memories. But every once in a while, there are moments that just won’t fade. When I look back on the years I spent in North Korea, it’s not really the tough days or frustrations that come to mind first. It’s the people. Their resilience. Their quiet kindness. The way they kept believing, even when things felt impossible.
There’s one memory I just can’t shake—a farewell dinner with my local colleagues. The feeling in the room was a mix of pride and sadness. We’d come so far together, and now it was time to say goodbye. As the night wound down, one colleague stood up, glass in hand, and said, “We are grateful for your friendship. You have shown us that the world is bigger than we imagined.” In that moment, all the things that usually divide us—language, politics, even history—just seemed to disappear. What was left was a real sense of connection.
Living in North Korea is a study in opposites—there’s hope and hardship, progress and setbacks, moments of real connection and long stretches of isolation. If you’ve ever experienced it, you know it’s a powerful reminder: change can happen, even in places where it seems least likely. Patience and empathy matter. And the human spirit? It’s stronger than we think.
The story doesn’t just stop when you leave. The friendships stick with you. The lessons keep shaping how you see the world. That hope for a brighter future—it lingers. If you’re willing to look past the headlines, you’ll see that North Korea is more than just a place of mystery or fear. It’s a country full of real people, big dreams, and endless possibilities.
